content.text: Signals and RxJS answer different questions. A signal holds a value you can read right now; an Observable delivers a sequence of events over time, with operators for waiting, cancelling and combining them. Move the state your templates read into signals, keep RxJS where timing and every single event matter, and connect the two with
After upgrading to Angular 22, a team adopts a rule: no Observables in components. The product search, built on
, becomes an effect that calls the API whenever

changes. Within a week, two bugs come in. Typing "laptop" sends a request for nearly every letter, and on a slow connection the results for "lap" sometimes arrive last and replace the results for "laptop".
The belief: signals are Angular's new reactivity and RxJS is the old one, so a modern app converts every Observable to a signal and stops using operators.
The direction of travel makes it look that way. Angular's newer APIs are signal-based:
pipe. And many Observables in Angular code really were state in disguise: a
that only existed to compute a total. Converting those is a genuine improvement. The mistake is the word "every". Some Observables were never state.
A signal is a value; an Observable is a sequence of events

always has a current value, and reading it is synchronous. When it changes, its consumers learn that they're stale, and each one reads whatever value is current when it runs. Two things follow. Setting a value equal to the current one, by
by default, notifies nobody. And values set between two reads are never seen: the interop guide sets a signal to 1, 2 and 3 in a row, and
pushes every emission to its subscribers, in order, and it has a notion of time: it can complete or fail, and operators can wait (

), merge or retry. So the useful question isn't "old or new?" but "state or event?". The current query, the selected product and the cart are state: only the latest value matters. A keystroke you want to wait out, a request that a newer one supersedes, a WebSocket message or a click you must count are events: each occurrence, and when it happened, matters.

The query is state, so a signal is the right home for it. "Fetch results for the latest query, but not on every keystroke, and ignore responses that arrive too late" is about events over time. An effect has no timing operators, and nothing cancels the previous request when a new one starts.

How to apply it in your project
For each one, ask: does anyone care about anything but the latest value? If not, it's state. If every emission or its timing matters, it's an event stream.

Signals skip intermediate values and ignore equal ones: right for state, wrong for events.
